newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS-Aussie debt still gets thumbs up in US.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Aussie debt still gets thumbs up in US.

text.p: U.S. investors remain unabashedly upbeat on Australian bonds, even after a monthly central bank bulletin diminished hopes for an imminent interest rate cut and sparked a sell-off in the debt market this week, experts said.
"We were pretty bullish on Australia to begin with," said Julie Grandstaff, a vice president of global fixed-income at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser.
"So, we look at this back-up as a buying opportunity if you're not already at your maximum levels," she said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) October report released on Wednesday warned that some recent wage agreements were based on higher than actual inflation levels and a premature rate cut could generate problems for the future.

Prior to the RBA bulletin, economists had widely believed a 50 basis point rate cut was possible after the release of inflation and wage data next week or more likely after the central bank's monthly board meeting on November 5.
The yield spread on 10-year Australian bonds to comparable U.S. Treasuries hovered near 112 basis points on Thursday compared with less than 100 at the start of the week.

Sluggish Australian economic growth, a favorable inflation outlook, lingering belief that rates will eventually head lower and appetite for higher yields help preserve U.S. investors' faith in Aussie paper, experts said.
J.P. Morgan economist Brian Gendreau predicted the Australian economy probably contracted by slightly less than 1.0 percent in the third quarter.
There is still enough softness in the Australian economy to lower Australian bond spreads further, the J.P. Morgan vice president said.
"Our view is that the RBA is going to continue to ease policy by 50 basis points this year and another 25 basis points in the first half of next year," Gendreau said.
A desperate search for higher yields as rates in Germany and Japan have tumbled this year should also support Australian bonds going forward, according to experts.
Bargain hunters have made a bee-line for the more generous yields in peripheral European bonds, tightening spreads since the start of this year.
Relative to some European bonds that have already rallied sharply, Australian bonds offer good value based on their nominal yield and inflation prospects, Grandstaff said.
The RBA bulletin which appeared to cause consternation in some circles soothed U.S. investors, inspiring confidence in the central bank's resolve to keep inflation in check.

"Once the market digests all this information, the positive sign is ... (Ian) Macfarlane who heads the RBA is not inclined to cut rates just because the market wants it," said John Krey, chief investment strategist for Barclays Private Bank. "He's an inflation fighter."
Dampened expectations for a rate cut have supported the Australian dollar, which traded near $0.7925/30 in the late afternoon, up from $0.7914/19 at the open.
Krey also drew positive implications for Australian bonds from the Aussie dollar's steady performance.
"It's full throttle ahead for the Australian bond market as long as the currency remains stable," he said.
